verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster: Al-tashchet. Of David. A miktam.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster. To the tune called "Do Not Destroy." David's. A miktam.
verses.directors_commentary: This is not part of the performance; it is the label on the scroll. The KJV does not number it at all, which is why every verse after it is one ahead of the KJV's. Three of the four terms are a performance note: למנצח, 'for the choirmaster', hands the psalm to the temple musicians; אל תשחת, 'do not destroy', is most likely the name of a melody (it heads Psalms 57, 58, 59 and 75), though the Targum and Malbim read it as David's own cry to God not to destroy him, and Radak ties it to the spared Saul. מכתם is a word nobody can pin down. The KJV left it untranslated as 'Michtam'; YLT guesses 'a secret treasure', from כֶּתֶם, 'gold'. Rashi gives only 'a pleasant song'. The 'of David' is a dedication or attribution, not a stage direction: the Hebrew preposition לְ can mean 'by', 'for' or 'belonging to'. Director's note: the old readers tied the psalm to David and Saul's court, but the text itself names no scene.

philological_notes.note: 'Do not destroy', a prohibition (jussive of שחת). It is either a tune name or an inscribed prayer; the text does not say which.
A psalm-type word of unknown meaning. Rashi calls it a pleasant song; the link to 'gold' (כֶּתֶם) is a guess, not a result.

verses.translation_literal: Really, [in] silence, righteousness do you speak? Uprightness do you judge, sons of man?
verses.translation_dramatic: Is it true? You who stand mute, do you speak righteousness? Do you judge with uprightness, you sons of men?
verses.directors_commentary:
The opening word is a challenge, and the voice should be sharp: הַאֻמְנָם, 'really? in truth?' The whole line turns on one ambiguous word, אֵלֶם, which can be read as 'silence' (the ASV's 'in silence', YLT's 'O dumb one') or as 'assembly', a gathering bound together like the sheaves of Genesis 37:7 (Ibn Ezra reports this as the view of some; Meiri adopts it, hearing in it the assembly of judges). The KJV chose the second and wrote 'O congregation', which flattens the sound-play between speaking and silence; the Hebrew sets 'silence' next to 'righteousness you speak', which can be heard as bitter irony: those whose duty was to speak right are mute. BBE's 'gods' rests on a changed vowel, not on this text.

The tradition gives the speech a concrete setting. Rashi and Metzudat David place it in Saul's camp, where David took the spear and water jug and called across to Abner, 'Will you not answer?' (1 Samuel 26:14): those around Saul were silent when they should have spoken the truth that David was not Saul's enemy. Meiri instead pictures the court itself. In either setting the charge is that men whose office is to speak justice and to judge (שפט) evenly do neither. Malbim hears a contrast between what the mouth says and what the heart and hands do, which the next verse spells out.

philological_notes.note: Read three ways: 'silence' (from אלם 'be mute'), 'assembly' (from אלם 'bind', as in אֲלֻמִּים 'sheaves', Gen 37:7), or emended to אֵלִים 'gods'. The KJV's 'congregation' and the ASV's 'in silence' show the split in English.
The interrogative ה plus אֻמְנָם 'truly, really': a rhetorical question that expects 'no'. From the root of faithfulness; Rashi glosses it as a word of אֱמוּנָה.

verses.translation_literal: Even in [the] heart you do injustices; in the land the violence of your hands you weigh out.
verses.translation_dramatic: No. In the heart you are already at work, and the work is crooked. And out in the land you set your violent hands on the scales and weigh it out, as if it were fair measure.
verses.directors_commentary: The accusation moves from speech to heart to hands, and the last verb is a trader's. תְּפַלֵּסוּן is 'you level, you weigh out': these judges do not merely commit violence, they put it on a balance and hand it out as a just portion. The KJV's 'ye weigh the violence of your hands' keeps the verb but gives no reason why a reader should feel the sting; the point is that the scales, the symbol of fairness in every market in the ancient Near East, are used for injustice. Radak and Ibn Ezra read it as making violence look level; Rashi, as tipping the balance towards it. The KJV also turns the plural עוֹלֹת into the abstract 'wickedness'; the Hebrew has 'injustices', many separate acts, each worked out in the mind. Note אַף, 'even': the heart is the first stage of the workshop, not a hidden vice.

philological_notes.note: 'You weigh out, you level'. The noun פֶּלֶס is a balance or level. The sense is violence handed out by measure.
Plural of עַוְלָה, 'injustice'; Rashi lists it beside עֲוָלוֹת, with the vav written for the plural.

verses.translation_literal: Estranged are the wicked from [the] womb; they go astray from [the] belly, speakers of lie.
verses.translation_dramatic: From the womb they were already turning aside, the wicked; from the very belly they wandered. They speak lies.
verses.directors_commentary:
The poet uses birth as a figure of how deep the wrongdoing runs: nothing in the Hebrew says more than 'from the womb' and 'from the belly', two parallel phrases for the start of life. The KJV's 'as soon as they be born' is a fair gloss, but it turns a poetic doubling into a timetable; a modern reader should hear hyperbole, the way we say someone was 'born to it'. The verbs also repeat the idea: זרו, 'they are estranged' (from the root זוּר, the same root as זָר, 'stranger'), and תעו, 'they wander', two images of leaving the path. Ibn Ezra notes that the second verb doubles the sense of the first, and Radak calls it a repetition in different words.

Who are they estranged from? Rashi and Metzudat David say from God, 'made strangers to the Holy One', Rashi pointing to Esau, whose twins struggled within Rebekah (Genesis 25:22); Ibn Ezra and Meiri keep it simpler, 'strange from the day of their birth'. Only Malbim presses the two verbs apart: the wicked turn aside once born, but the liars went astray 'from the belly', before birth; that distinction is his, not the text's. Finally, the verse ends with a participle, 'speakers of lie', so the KJV's 'speaking lies' is correct but loses that it names a kind of person, not an act.

philological_notes.note: A past form of זוּר 'turn aside, be estranged', from the same root as זָר 'stranger, outsider'. Rashi explains it as a passive-sense form, like שֹׁמּוּ in Jer 2:12.
'Lie, falsehood'. With the participle דֹּבְרֵי it names the habitual speaker of lies, which Metzudat David applies to David's slanderers.

verses.translation_literal: Venom [is] theirs, like the likeness of the venom of a snake, like a deaf cobra [that] shuts its ear,
verses.translation_dramatic: Venom is in them, the very likeness of the serpent's venom. Like the cobra that has gone deaf, that stops its own ear,
verses.directors_commentary: Two snake images, both about poison and hearing. חֵמָה is both 'venom' and 'heat, rage', which is why English readers feel it drift between the two; the KJV picks 'poison' and loses the fury. The פֶּתֶן is a cobra or similar snake; the KJV's 'adder' is a European snake and a poor fit for the Near East, where cobras were known from Egypt. The deafness is the punchline: ancient Near Eastern snake-charmers sang spells to calm snakes, and a snake that will not listen is beyond control. Rashi gives a folk idea that the old snake turns one ear against the ground and stops the other with dust. The KJV's 'stoppeth her ear' invents a feminine snake: the Hebrew has 'his ear', masculine. The wicked are as deaf to a warning as a cobra to its charmer.

philological_notes.note: A venomous snake, usually taken as a cobra; the Egyptian cobra was the royal uraeus. KJV and ASV 'adder' is a guess from the English fauna.
'Shuts, stops up' (an ear). Metzudat Zion cites Proverbs 21:13, 'stops his ear'.

verses.translation_literal: [one] that does not listen to the voice of whisperers, a caster of spells, skilled.
verses.translation_dramatic: That will not hear the voice of the whisperers, though the one who weaves the spell is a master of his craft.
verses.directors_commentary: The sentence continues from the last verse; in performance, do not drop your voice at the verse break. מְלַחֲשִׁים is 'whisperers', and the Hebrew sound is meant: the charmers' craft is quiet, murmured, hissing, la-cha-shim, as if the word were itself a spell. The KJV's 'charmers' is fair, but 'charming never so wisely' is archaic, and the Hebrew is bluntly 'a spell-caster, skilled', with חוֹבֵר חֲבָרִים repeating the root: 'a binder of bindings'. The same figure is in Deuteronomy 18:11, in the list of forbidden practices, which tells us the psalmist is using a trade he knew, not praising it. Rashi (citing Shabbat 153b) says the phrase means one who knows how to charm snakes. The point is the failure: even the best expert gets no answer from the cobra, and no argument gets through to these judges.

philological_notes.note: 'One who binds bindings', a spell-caster; the same root as 'to join, tie'. The phrase recurs in Deuteronomy 18:11 among the forbidden practices.

verses.translation_literal: God, break their teeth in their mouth; the fangs of young lions, tear down, YHWH.
verses.translation_dramatic: O God! Break their teeth, there in their mouths. The fangs of these young lions, tear them out, O LORD.
verses.directors_commentary: The mood turns from description to prayer, and from snake to lion: the same mouths now have teeth. The prayer opens with the divine name אֱלֹהִים and closes with YHWH, a frame the KJV preserves ('O God' ... 'O Lord'), but its 'O Lord' for YHWH hides the personal name. הֲרָס is 'break down', a verb used for walls and altars, and נְתֹץ is the same; the psalmist asks God to demolish the teeth like masonry. The מַלְתְּעוֹת are the great back teeth, the ones that crush; Rashi's French gloss is 'molars'. Malbim sees the teeth as the slander by which they seize their prey. The KJV's 'young lions' is right but softens the image: כְּפִירִים are lions old enough to hunt, which is exactly why they are dangerous. In the setting of Psalms, a lion with its teeth gone cannot kill: the violence is asked to be disarmed, not only avenged.

philological_notes.note: The large jaw-teeth, fangs or molars; Rashi glosses them as inner teeth, Metzudat Zion relates the word to מְתַלְּעוֹת in Proverbs 30:14.
Young but full-grown lions, hunting age. Ibn Ezra explains the comparison: the wicked tear with their mouths.

verses.translation_literal: May they melt away like water; may they go about for themselves; may he tread his arrows, as if they were cut off.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them melt like water and run off, wandering where the current takes them. Let him draw his bow, and let them be cut down, withered.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speech now turns from accusation to curse, and the voice drops into a steady, almost quiet cadence. Three images follow: water, a bow, a stalk. The first verb, יִמָּאֲסוּ, is hard. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat Zion take the alef as standing in for a doubled letter, so that it means 'melt' (מסס), the same word as in 'the people's heart melted'; this is the KJV's 'melt away'. Rashi reads it as 'may they become loathsome to themselves', from מאס, which is a different image. The plural 'they go about for themselves' (יִתְהַלְּכוּ־לָמוֹ) then describes water spreading with no direction; the KJV's 'which run continually' pins it to the water rather than to the wicked, and the Hebrew is not that explicit.

The second half has a singular verb with no named subject: 'he treads his arrows', where 'treads' is the usual verb for stringing a bow, since the archer steps on it. Rashi and Metzudat David say God; Radak says each wicked man draws his bow against David, the bow being the mouth and the arrows their words. The KJV's 'when he bendeth his bow to shoot his arrows' adds a bow and a shooting the Hebrew only implies. The last word, יִתְמֹלָלוּ, 'cut off', recalls the grass that is 'cut off and dries up' in Psalm 90; Malbim hears it as the arrows' tips being snapped off, the KJV 'cut in pieces' as the wicked being sliced. Either way the aim is that the harm they would do is broken before it lands. The text has a Ketiv/Qere here: the written חצו ('his arrow') is read as חציו, 'his arrows'.

philological_notes.note: The alef takes the place of a doubled letter, so the word is 'they melt' (from מסס), as in וימס לבב העם; Rashi alone takes it from מאס as 'become loathsome'. The STEPBible gloss 'may they flow' is a looser rendering of the same melting image.
'Be cut off, wither', the same root as in ימולל ויבש of Psalm 90:6; Meiri takes it as 'as if cut off', so that they cannot do harm.

verses.translation_literal: Like a snail [that] melts away, it goes; a miscarriage of a woman, [they] have not seen the sun.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them be like a snail that dissolves as it crawls; like a woman's untimely child, that never saw the sun.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two small, intimate pictures of vanishing, each linked to the sun, the Bible's figure for the light of life. A snail leaves a slime trail and seems to shrink as it crawls; Ibn Ezra reports ancient writers saying the snail melts as it goes, and Radak says it hides in its shell. תֶּמֶס is a one-time noun, 'a melting', so the KJV's 'which melteth' is right in sense, though the closing 'let every one of them pass away' is the KJV's addition, drawn from 'it goes' (יַהֲלֹךְ), where the Hebrew has only a singular verb.

The second image is the heavier one, and the line needs a pause before it. נֵפֶל אֵשֶׁת is 'a woman's miscarriage', the construct form אֵשֶׁת standing for אִשָּׁה (Ibn Ezra and Meiri); Radak and Meiri read it so, as does the KJV's 'untimely birth of a woman'. Rashi gives first an animal instead: a blind burrowing creature (טַלְפָּ״א, rendered אֲשׁוּתָא in Targum on Leviticus 11:30), which is how the rabbis explained it (Moed Katan 6b), and offers the miscarriage as 'some say'; Meiri lists the creature as 'some interpret'. Both the snail and the miscarriage are things that never reach the light, so the point does not change. The KJV's 'that they may not see the sun' turns a plural past verb, 'they have not seen', into a purpose clause; Meiri notes the plural is for all of them together.

philological_notes.note: 'A woman's miscarriage' (נפל 'that which fell', with a construct אֵשֶׁת for אִשָּׁה, as in אֵשֶׁת יְפַת תֹּאַר). Rashi's first reading is a blind burrowing creature, the 'mole' of the rabbis; the miscarriage is the alternative in Rashi, and the main reading in Radak and Meiri.
'Snail, slug' (Radak, Meiri, Metzudat Zion). Rashi offers an alternative: a doubled form of שִׁבֹּלֶת מַיִם, a flood or current, which Ibn Ezra also finds possible.

verses.translation_literal: Before your pots perceive [the] thornbush, as living, as burning, he will whirl [it] away.
verses.translation_dramatic: Before your pots can feel the thorn-fire beneath them, a whirlwind will sweep it all away, the raw and the scorched alike.
verses.directors_commentary:
A kitchen scene. A cooking pot sits on a fire of thorn-brush, which burns hot and fast and dies as fast: the psalmist's image of how quickly a wicked man's heat will go out. Brush fuel, אָטָד, is the same 'thornbush' that offers itself as king of the trees in Judges 9:15. 'Before your pots perceive' uses the verb בין, 'discern', so the pots are given the sense a cook has when the water starts to warm; the KJV's 'can feel' smooths that into plain sensation, and 'thorns' hides that the Hebrew has the singular 'thornbush'.

Two words in this verse are contested, and an actor should know which choice is being made. First, סִירֹתֵיכֶם: Radak, Meiri, Malbim and the KJV take it as 'your pots'; Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David take it as young thorn shoots, the wicked's children, which have not yet hardened into thornbushes. Second, כְּמוֹ חַי כְּמוֹ חָרוֹן. Radak and Malbim read the meat in the pot, raw (חַי) versus scorched (חָרוֹן), so that the whirlwind strikes before the meat has cooked, raw or scorched alike. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David read it as 'in strength and in burning anger' with God as the one who tears them out, as a man in fury uproots a tree. The KJV's 'in his wrath' reads the second way but supplies 'his', which the Hebrew does not have, and its 'both living' is stiff beside ASV's 'the green and the burning alike'. The verb ישערנו, 'he whirls it away' (שׂעַר, a storm wind), is singular both for the 'it' taken away and for the unnamed 'he'; Meiri says prophetic speech shifts between singular and plural, and between 'he' and 'you'.

philological_notes.note: Disputed. Burning anger: Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Metzudat David. Scorched, burnt meat set against raw (חַי): Radak and Malbim. The KJV's 'his wrath' supplies the pronoun.
'Your pots' (סִיר) in Radak, Meiri, Malbim; 'your thorn shoots' (סִירִים, as in Nahum 1:10) in Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion.
A thornbush, here the fuel under the pot; the same word as in Judges 9:15.

verses.translation_literal: The righteous will rejoice that he has seen vengeance; his steps he will wash in [the] blood of the wicked.
verses.translation_dramatic: The righteous will rejoice, for he has seen the avenging. He will wash his feet in the blood of the wicked.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the verse that modern readers flinch at, and the director should not let the actor soften it. פְּעָמָיו is 'his steps' (the Hebrew word for footfalls), and the KJV's 'he shall wash his feet' is acceptable but plainer than the original. The image is the battlefield after victory: in the Near East a conqueror's feet were stained with the blood of the field, and the picture belongs to war poems like Psalm 68:24 and Isaiah 63:3. The vengeance is God's; the righteous man is a witness, not the killer. The KJV's 'shall rejoice when he seeth' makes the joy follow the sight; the Hebrew נָקָם is 'vengeance' (Metzudat David: the vengeance of the LORD), and the verb חָזָה is the seer's word, as in a vision. Meiri calls the bathing an exaggeration, a way of saying how large the vengeance is. In the psalm's own movement this is the end of the curse, and the beginning of the last line of the poem, where the reason for the joy is given.

philological_notes.note: 'Vengeance, redress', the legal word for righting a wrong, not private spite. Metzudat David ties it to the LORD's vengeance.
'His steps, footfalls'; Metzudat Zion and Meiri read it as 'feet' as a stand-in for the whole walking man.

verses.translation_literal: And a human will say: Surely [there is] fruit for the righteous; surely there is God[s], judging on the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then people will say: There is fruit for the righteous after all. There is a God who judges on the earth.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm ends on an answer to its opening. It began by asking whether human judges speak righteously, and it ends with the world's verdict: there is a judge above the judges. אַךְ appears twice and is 'surely, after all', with the weight of a man who had doubted and was wrong; the KJV's 'Verily' is a good word, but its 'reward' for פְּרִי, 'fruit', loses the farming metaphor, which is the whole claim: righteousness is a crop that does come in. The last phrase is the same plural-form word אֱלֹהִים used with a plural participle, שֹׁפְטִים. The KJV hides this under 'a God that judgeth'. The commentators offer three solutions: plural of majesty (Radak), angels who carry out the judgment (Ibn Ezra, Radak), or, as the echo of verse 2 suggests, the true divine court that outranks the earthly one. A director should make the audience hear both the singular sense and the plural form. The speaker is not any particular person: אָדָם is 'a human, anyone', which links back to the 'sons of Adam' addressed in verse 2.

philological_notes.note: A plural-form divine name with a plural participle, 'God who judges' (plural of majesty) or 'gods who judge' (angels or a divine court).
'Fruit, produce': the harvest metaphor for the result of righteous life; KJV 'reward' flattens it.
